rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who seek the Hereafter and make the fitting effort succeed there while receiving whatever worldly share God ordained for them.
rows.anchor: these people who earn in this world whatever is ordained for them and the hereafter is already an abode of success for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Desire for the Hereafter alone is insufficient: it must be joined to fitting effort and faith free of polytheism.
rows.anchor: they also require a befitting effort and a faith too that is devoid of any stain of polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's bounty reaches both groups: worldly seekers receive their allotted share, while those who seek the Hereafter receive their worldly portion and the reward of their deeds there.
rows.anchor: The implication is that the Almighty’s bounties are available to everyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since worldly shares are allotted and the Hereafter offers lasting success, a person should not trade its abiding blessings for temporary worldly pleasures.
rows.anchor: deprive himself of the abiding blessings of the hereafter while becoming a slave to the pleasures of this trivial and temporary world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People cannot determine the amount of blessings they receive; God apportions them abundantly or sparingly.
rows.anchor: God has given abundantly to whomsoever He wanted and sparingly to whomsoever He wanted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the discussion turns aside from the original path announced in verse 9, this section resumes it: the Qur’an's way to God follows human nature and intellect and establishes justice and goodness; verses 22–39 explain 16:90.
rows.anchor: the path which the Qur’ ān outlines in leading people to God is explained. This is the straight path followed by human nature and intellect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular address can address every member of a group; any address to the Prophet here is as believers’ leader, not as an individual alone.
rows.anchor: it is in his capacity of the leader of the believers and the address is not specific to him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the verb fa-taq‘ud has the sense of other incomplete verbs in this construction.
rows.anchor: here has the same meaning as other incomplete verbs as

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God alone owns and provides livelihood, associating others in His divinity violates justice; the Qur’an likewise calls polytheism a great injustice.
rows.anchor: only God is the master and giver of livelihood, people should not associate others with Him in His rights and in His divinity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blame and abandonment are the consequence of shirk on the Day of Resurrection, whose locative is suppressed; people bear responsibility and their alleged deities will disown them.
rows.anchor: which is suppressed here. In other words, people themselves will be responsible of this fate. Not only will their alleged deities not help them, they will go on to curse them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone declares whether anyone shares His rights; even parents, despite their foremost human claim as the means of one's existence and nurture, are not to be worshipped and are owed kindness.
rows.anchor: After God, if there is anyone who has the greatest right, it is the parents.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ḥasanan is an emphatic object from an omitted verb, requiring the utmost kindness to parents.
rows.anchor: is a stressed object from a suppressed verb and would mean that parents should be treated with ultimate kindness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term describing impatience denotes aversion of the heart; the term for scolding is explained alongside the call to kind treatment.
rows.anchor: expresses aversion of the heart and

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term for scolding means to rebuke, and the following sentence explains the kindness required toward parents.
rows.anchor: means “to scold someone.” The sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Old age is singled out because children may then see parents as burdens and forget their sacrifices; parents deserve love, respect, and good conduct at every age.
rows.anchor: Old age has been specifically mentioned in the verse because it is this period in which people regard their parents to be a burden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous verse named the greatest justice, while this one names the greatest kindness, the Qur’an’s second foundational teaching.
rows.anchor: the greatest act of kindness is mentioned and is the second pillar of foundational teachings of the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse guides people who cannot meet the previously stated rights in how to respond to those seeking help.
rows.anchor: This is verse provides guidance to people in the case when they are not in a position to fulfil the rights just mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving kin their due is a binding obligation on every person with wealth, not merely a moral recommendation; failure violates others’ rights.
rows.anchor: the responsibility stated is not just a moral one; it is an obligation that must be fulfilled by every person who has wealth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kin are entitled by relationship, the needy by need, and a needy relative has both claims; placing the needy next also reflects their rank in Islamic society.
rows.anchor: Kinfolk become worthy of this right merely on the basis of kinship. For the needy, it is merely their need that makes them eligible for this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Travel itself makes a person eligible for help, even when the traveler is not needy in the juristic sense.
rows.anchor: a traveller becomes eligible just because he is travelling; it is not essential that he be in need

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because others have rights in one's wealth, one must spend cautiously and moderately on permissible needs and reserve the rest for those rights.
rows.anchor: a person should spend with moderation and caution on his permissible needs and regard himself to be responsible for the remaining wealth towards fulfilling the needs of others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gratitude for God’s favors means spending only on what pleases Him, while Satan tempts people to spend in ways that distance them from God.
rows.anchor: Satan lures people to his ways and makes them spend on things which take them further away from God and nearer to his own self.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tying the hand to the neck depicts extreme stinginess, while leaving it loose depicts squandering.
rows.anchor: Tying one’s hands to one’s neck signifies extreme stinginess and leaving them loose signifies squandering wealth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning against waste in verses 26–27, the verse prescribes balance: moderate spending on permissible needs and fulfillment of others’ rights, avoiding indigence that leaves them unmet.
rows.anchor: a person should spend with moderation on his permissible needs and also fulfil the rights of others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words meaning ‘to whom He pleases’ are omitted after ‘for’ because context makes them understood.
rows.anchor: are suppressed as well because of concomitant indications.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abundance and constriction of wealth depend on God’s will and wisdom, not human plans; He knows and watches His servants, so people should spend moderately and meet others’ rights.
rows.anchor: The constriction or abundance in wealth is not dependent on the plans of a person. It is dependent entirely on God’s will and wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God is the true sustainer, fear of poverty cannot justify killing children; the verse condemns the jāhiliyyah practice of burying girls and, in Islahi’s polemical view, the same sustenance-denying rationale behind modern family planning.
rows.anchor: The verse alludes to the evil Arab custom of burying alive infant girls in the time of jāhiliyyah. The psyche behind this was that since a woman was not an earning member of the family

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses through 31 address the commands in 16:90—justice, goodness, and kin spending—while the following verses turn to its prohibitions of lewdness, evil, and rebellion.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, the things proscribed – lewdness, evil and rebelliousness – are discussed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adultery is named first among the prohibitions because it destroys the family roots of a righteous society; true lineage and blood ties sustain natural and spiritual family bonds.
rows.anchor: Among the proscribed things, adultery is mentioned the foremost because this evil destroys the roots of a righteous society.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning not even to approach adultery bars its motives and precursors; Islahi says this verse states the principle while details will be explained later in Sūrah al-Nūr.
rows.anchor: people should stay away from things that may induce them to indulge in this shameful act.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its prohibition needs no proof because extra-marital relations are universally recognized as lewd; this deviant path uproots the upright family, society, and government.
rows.anchor: It is a universally acknowledged vulgarity. Ever since time immemorial, mankind has not condoned extra-marital relations between men and women.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person may be killed only when the sharī‘ah orders it for a crime; killing without that legal basis is grave injustice.
rows.anchor: A person can only be killed when the sharī‘ah orders for his killing because of some crime.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For unjust killing, the victim’s heirs may seek qiṣāṣ or diyah or forgive; they must not kill beyond the murderer or use prohibited methods such as burning or mutilation.
rows.anchor: the heirs of the victim have full authority to either take qiṣāṣ or diyat or even forgive the perpetrator.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heirs are the primary claimants and the government enforces their choice, intervening as claimant only when there are no heirs or they decline; Islahi says current laws deprive Islamic law of blessings and refers to his other book.
rows.anchor: the real claimants in murder are the heirs of the victim and not the government. The only job of the latter is to correctly enforce the will of the former.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guardians may use an orphan’s wealth only for upbringing, development, and protection; they must hand it over when the orphan reaches maturity.
rows.anchor: Only that intervention of their guardians in their wealth is permissible which is done for their upbringing, development and protection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Promises include written and naturally understood covenants; they must be fulfilled unless contrary to sharī‘ah, and social institutions depend on keeping them.
rows.anchor: Included in these covenants are all types of promises whether they are written or naturally understood. Whatever their nature, if they are not against the sharī‘ah, they must be fulfilled.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dishonesty in measures may seem profitable to individuals but destroys the truth and justice on which an upright society depends.
rows.anchor: they raze down the foundation of truthfulness and justice which guarantees the continued existence of an upright society.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression qafawtu atharahu means ‘I came following it.’
rows.anchor: means “I came following it.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse bars following conjectures without knowledge, including slander and rumor that injure reputations; Qur’anic society rests on trust and giving others the benefit of the doubt.
rows.anchor: The society which the Qur’an wants to create is founded on trust and giving others the benefit of the doubt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word marah means walking arrogantly, with feet stamping and the neck raised high.
rows.anchor: means “to walk arrogantly.” A person who walks in this manner, walks while stamping his feet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth and towering mountains display human smallness before God; a person should recognize his station and submit humbly to divine majesty.
rows.anchor: what is the meaning of being arrogant before Him? One should try to recognize one’s status and always surrender oneself to the majesty and splendour of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Outward arrogant manner reflects an inner failure to grasp God’s power and majesty; those who grasp it are humble and down to earth.
rows.anchor: this external mannerism of a person reflects his inner-self. It is a proof of the fact that such a person has no conception of God’s power and majesty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhālik refers to all the preceding teachings, which are sound, lasting truths rooted in intellect, human nature, and sharī‘ah, conveyed through the Messenger to guide life.
rows.anchor: All of them are a part of wisdom. In other words, they are sound and abiding truths which have strong foundations in a person’s intellect, nature and in the sharī‘ah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism frames this section: it begins in verse 22 and ends by repeating that worship belongs to God alone; preserving this enclosing frame preserves the teachings, as other Qur’anic and Torah passages also do.
rows.anchor: It was also discussed in verse 22 from where this section of verses actually began. It is as if it is being said that as long as this wall formed of monotheism that encircles these teachings is intact, the teachings themselves are intact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next section identifies Quraysh’s aversion as resistance to abandoning their claimed deities and accepting the Hereafter, and instructs Muslims to preach wisely without provoking greater aversion.
rows.anchor: Since they were not willing to giving up their self-claimed deities and accept the hereafter, they had this dislike for the Qur’ ān and the Prophet (sws).
